name: CH32V307VCT6
title: CH32V303/305/307/317 32-bit RISC-V (QingKe V4F) microcontrollers, 144 MHz, USB HS PHY, Ethernet
summary: A family of 32-bit microcontrollers built on the QingKe V4F RISC-V core (RV32IMAFC with a single-precision FPU) running at up to 144 MHz with no flash wait states in the fast region. Members carry up to 480 KB of code flash, up to 128 KB of SRAM, two 12-bit ADCs, two 12-bit DACs, four op-amp/comparators, up to eight U(S)ARTs, two CAN, USB full-speed host/device and OTG, a USB 2.0 high-speed controller with its own 480 Mbit/s PHY, SDIO, FSMC and a camera port. The CH32V307 adds a gigabit Ethernet MAC with a built-in 10 Mbit/s PHY; the CH32V317 has a built-in 10/100 Mbit/s PHY. The CH32V307VCT6 is the 100-pin LQFP member with 80 GPIO.
key_figures: 480 KB (CH32V305FB/GB: 224 KB), of which 128/256 KB zero-wait by default
32 KB or 64 KB default, configurable up to 128 KB (192 KB on some lots)
VDD 2.4 to 3.6 V; 3.0 to 3.6 V when USB or Ethernet is used
22.4 mA typ at 144 MHz, all peripherals on (HSE)
up to 80, FT pins 5 V tolerant

operation.text: The QingKe V4F core executes RV32IMAFC with single-precision floating point, single-cycle multiply and hardware divide (5-cycle integer division). It has machine and user privilege levels, standard memory protection, static or dynamic branch prediction, custom extended instructions and a 2-wire serial debug port (SDI).

The fast programmable interrupt controller (PFIC) handles up to 255 vectors; 8 core-private and 88 peripheral interrupts are used. It offers a non-maskable interrupt, a hardware stack saving context with no instruction cost, 4 vector-table-free fast channels, address or instruction vector tables, nesting up to 8 levels and tail-chaining. EXTI has 19 edge detectors; any of up to 80 GPIOs map onto its 16 external lines, each with rising, falling or both-edge triggers and its own mask.

SRAM is up to 128 KB and is lost at power-down. Code flash is up to 480 KB, split into a zero-wait execution area and a wait-state area whose sizes depend on the part and the option word. A 28 KB system flash holds the factory bootloader, which can reprogram code flash over USART1 or USB. There are 128 bytes of factory configuration (not user-writable) and 128 bytes of user option bytes.

BOOT0 and BOOT1 (on PB2) choose at start-up between code flash, system memory (bootloader) and internal SRAM. On packages without a BOOT0 pin it is tied to ground inside; where BOOT1/PB2 is not bonded it is tied to ground inside, or floats if BOOT0 is also missing, and a pull-down input setting on PB2 then saves current in low-power modes.

VDD (2.4 to 3.6 V) feeds some I/O and the internal regulators, including the USB and Ethernet PHYs. VIO (2.4 to 3.6 V) feeds most I/O and sets their output high level; it must not exceed VDD in operation. VDDA powers the analog blocks: ADC, DAC, op-amps, PLL, HSI oscillator and temperature sensor; it must equal VIO, stay powered with VIO if VDD is off, and be at least 2.4 V with the ADC running. VBAT (1.8 to 3.6 V) takes over the RTC, LSE and backup registers through an internal switch when VDD is off. On the CH32V317, VDD_ETH (3.15 to 3.45 V) powers the 10/100M PHY and takes 1 to 4.7 µF to ground, or 10 µF with 0.1 µF in parallel, and VDDK is the core LDO's decoupling node needing 1 µF.

Bit VLEVEL in FEATURE_SIGN marks the supply range. With VLEVEL = 1, VDD, VIO and VDDA need 2.4 V minimum. With VLEVEL = 0, VDD and VDDA go down to 1.8 V and VIO to 1.8 V, or 1.2 V on lots whose fifth-from-last digit is above 4 (except parts without separate VIO and the CH32V305GBU6). The ADC, DAC and OPA still need 2.4 V.

Power-on/power-down reset is always active and holds the chip in reset below VPOR/PDR, so no external reset part is needed. The programmable voltage detector, enabled in software, compares VDD with one of 8 thresholds and can interrupt on crossing in either direction.
The core regulator is on after reset. In Stop mode it can drop to a low-power mode; in Standby it is switched off and its output goes high impedance.

Sleep stops only the CPU clock and wakes on any interrupt or event. Stop turns off the PLL, HSI and HSE and puts the flash in low-power mode while SRAM and registers are kept; it wakes on any EXTI event (16 I/O lines, PVD, RTC alarm, Ethernet or USB wake-up), NRST or an IWDG reset. Standby turns off the main LDO, flash and digital logic, keeping only the wake-up logic on a low-power LDO; up to 32 KB of SRAM and the backup registers can be kept. Leaving Standby is a reset with SBF set in PWR_CSR (cleared by CSBF); wake sources are EXTI events, NRST, IWDG and a rising edge on WKUP. After Stop or Standby the system clock is HSI.

Four sources: 8 MHz HSI RC (factory trimmed, default after reset), about 40 kHz LSI RC, 3 to 25 MHz HSE and 32.768 kHz LSE. The PLL multiplies HSI or HSE up to a 144 MHz system clock; HB, PB1 and PB2 each run up to 144 MHz. PLL2 and PLL3 serve the Ethernet and I2S clocks; PLL3 lets I2S reach every standard rate from 8 to 192 kHz. With clock security on, a failed HSE switches the system to HSI, stops HSE and the PLL and can raise an interrupt. MCO can output HSE, HSI, PLLCLK/2, PLL2, PLL3, PLL3/2 or XTI.
USB needs a 48 MHz clock divided from the main PLL, so the PLL must run at 48, 96 or 144 MHz when USBFS or OTG_FS is used.

The RTC is a 32-bit counter with a 20-bit prescaler clocked from LSE, LSI or HSE/128. It sits in the backup domain, powered from VDD or automatically from VBAT. 42 16-bit backup registers (84 bytes) survive Standby, system reset and power reset, and are cleared when tamper detection fires.

PC13, PC14 and PC15 are powered through the backup switch, which passes at most 3 mA. Under VDD, PC14/PC15 work as GPIO or LSE and PC13 as GPIO, TAMPER, RTC calibration clock, alarm or second output. As outputs they run at 2 MHz or less, drive at most 30 pF and must not source current such as LED drive. Under VBAT only the LSE and the PC13 tamper/RTC functions work. Their state after the first backup power-up is controlled by the backup registers, not by system reset.

Two 12-bit ADCs share up to 16 external and 2 internal channels (temperature sensor on IN16 and the internal reference). Single, continuous, scan and discontinuous modes, dual-ADC modes, an analog watchdog, timer or pin triggers and DMA are supported. The touch-key unit reuses up to 16 ADC channels; software decides the key state from the converted results.
Two 12-bit voltage DACs convert independently or together, triggered by timers or EXTI line 9, with triangle and noise generation and DMA.

Four 16-bit advanced timers (TIM1, TIM8, TIM9, TIM10) give 6-channel three-phase PWM with complementary outputs, dead-time, repetition counter and break input. Four 16-bit general timers (TIM2 to TIM5) each have 4 channels for capture, compare, PWM and one-pulse, read quadrature encoders and 1 to 3 Hall sensors, and freeze in debug. Two basic timers (TIM6, TIM7) can clock the DAC. The 12-bit independent watchdog runs from LSI and keeps going in Stop and Standby; it can be started by software or by option byte. The 7-bit window watchdog runs from the main clock and gives an early-warning interrupt. The core's 64-bit SysTick counts up or down. TIM2_CH1 and TIM2_ETR share one pin and cannot be used at the same time.

USART1 to USART3 and UART4 to UART8: full duplex, synchronous one-way and single-wire half duplex, LIN, ISO7816 smart card, IrDA SIR, CTS/RTS flow control, multiprocessor mode, fractional baud generator and DMA.

Up to 3 SPIs, master or slave, full or half duplex, multi-master, 8- or 16-bit frames, hardware CRC, SD/MMC basic mode and DMA. SPI2 and SPI3 double as I2S: 16/32-bit frames, 4 audio standards, 8 kHz to 562.2 kHz sampling and a master clock output at 256 × fs.
Two I2C interfaces, standard and fast mode, multi-master or slave, 7- or 10-bit addressing with dual 7-bit slave address, hardware PEC, SMBus 2.0 and PMBus, DMA.

CAN 2.0A/2.0B active up to 1 Mbit/s with time-triggered mode, 3 transmit mailboxes and two 3-deep receive FIFOs. Parts with two controllers share 28 filters and 512 bytes of SRAM; a part with one controller has 14 filters and shares its 512 bytes with USBD, which may then use only the lower 384 bytes.

USBFS is a full-speed host/device controller with 16 configurable endpoints and a host endpoint set, supporting control, bulk, isochronous and interrupt transfers, double buffering, suspend/resume and wake-up. OTG_FS can act as host and device and meets the OTG supplement 1.3, configurable as host only, device only or dual role.

USBHS works as host or device at USB 2.0 rates and has its own 480 Mbit/s PHY. As host it handles low, full and high-speed devices and high-speed hubs; as device it runs low, full or high speed with 16 endpoint numbers. Endpoints other than 0 take packets up to 1024 bytes with optional double buffering.
An 8, 10 or 12-bit parallel camera input synchronised by VSYNC and HSYNC, taking raw line/frame formats such as YUV and RGB or compressed JPEG streams, with cropping.
SDIO host for MMC, SD memory, SDIO and CE-ATA with 1, 4 or 8-bit data, up to 48 MHz in 8-bit mode; compatible with MMC 4.2, SD I/O 2.0, SD memory 2.0 and CE-ATA 1.1.
The external memory controller drives SRAM, PSRAM, NOR and NAND with 8, 16 or 32-bit accesses and adjustable timing, and can talk to LCD controllers in Intel 8080 or Motorola 6800 mode.

An IEEE 802.3 MAC at 10/100/1000 Mbit/s full duplex with MII, RMII and RGMII to an external PHY managed over SMI, hardware IPv4/IPv6, IP/ICMP/UDP/TCP checksum and frame padding, and several MAC address filters. The CH32V307 uses either its internal 10 Mbit/s PHY or an external gigabit PHY. The CH32V317 has an internal 10/100 Mbit/s PHY with automatic MDI/MDIX and polarity correction on both pairs.

Five ports with up to 80 pins, each set as push-pull or open-drain output, input with or without pull-up/pull-down, or peripheral function. All pins except those with analog functions have high current capability. A lock mechanism freezes the configuration. Most pins are powered from VIO, so VIO sets the interface logic level.

A CRC unit computes a fixed-polynomial CRC on 32-bit words, two DMA controllers give 18 channels (memory and peripherals, circular buffers) arbitrated with the CPU for SRAM, a true random number generator gives 32-bit values, and each chip carries a 96-bit unique ID.

Four op-amps, each usable as a comparator, with selectable input and output channels tied internally to the ADC and timers: small signals can be amplified into the ADC, and comparator results go to a GPIO or straight to a timer input.
The 2-wire SDI uses SWDIO and SWCLK and is on after power-up or reset; firmware can turn it off.

When certain peripherals are enabled together, some defaults move: SDIO_D0/D1 go from PC8/PC9 to PB14/PB15 with ETHMACEN and SDIOEN set; DVP_D5 goes from PB6 to PB3 and FSMC_NADV from PB7 to PD2 when USBHS is enabled with DVP or FSMC and RB_UC_RST_SIE = 0; I2S3_SD moves from PB5 to PA9 and I2S3_MCK from PC7 to PA8 when 10M Ethernet and I2S3 run together; SPI3_MOSI moves from PB5 to PA15 with Ethernet on the lots below, where the I2S3 default pins and the SPI3 chip select are unavailable. The SDIO, DVP and FSMC moves apply to lots whose fifth-from-last digit is above 1 or sixth-from-last digit is not 0 (the SDIO move excepts the CH32V305GBU6; on the CH32V317 the SDIO and DVP moves have no lot condition); the I2S3 moves to lots with fifth-from-last digit above 2 or sixth-from-last not 0; the SPI3_MOSI move to lots with fifth-from-last digit equal to 2 or sixth-from-last equal to 0.
